title: Plant adaptations: roots, stems and leaves

oak.lesson: Adaptations of plants for photosynthesis: absorbing light

big_idea: Roots, stems and leaves are adapted to supply every cell with water, mineral salts, light and carbon dioxide.
goals: I can describe what plants need from the soil and the air, and how roots, root hair cells and xylem are adapted to supply water and mineral salts.
I can explain how a leaf and its palisade cells are adapted for photosynthesis.

keywords.meaning: substances dissolved in soil water that plants need to stay healthy, e.g. nitrates
a mineral salt that supplies nitrogen for making proteins
an element plants need to make chlorophyll
an element root cells need to absorb water properly
a root cell with a long extension that gives a large surface area for absorbing water
hollow tubes made from dead cells that carry water and mineral salts up the plant
to droop because the cells have too little water
a leaf cell near the upper surface that is packed with chloroplasts
the outer layer of cells of a leaf
the waxy layer on a leaf that stops it losing too much water
the total area of the outside of something

misconceptions: Plants get their food from the soil. Plants get water and mineral salts from the soil, but they make their food (glucose) by photosynthesis in the leaves.
Mineral salts are food. They are not an energy source: nitrates are used to build proteins and magnesium to build chlorophyll.
Students do not link the shape of a structure to its job. Every adaptation here (root hairs, hollow xylem, thin broad leaves, chloroplast-packed palisade cells) is a shape that fits a function.
safety: No practical hazards beyond normal classroom rules.

slides.subtitle: How is a plant built to collect water, mineral salts, light and carbon dioxide?
slides.notes: Lesson 2 of 9B. Last lesson: the two reactions. This lesson: the structures that supply them, from root hair to palisade cell.

slides.title: Do Now: where do the reactants come from?
prompt: 1. Write the word equation for photosynthesis.
2. Which reactant comes from the air, and which comes from the soil?
3. Name two other things a plant needs that it gets from the soil.
slides.notes: Answers: carbon dioxide + water makes glucose + oxygen; carbon dioxide from the air, water from the soil; mineral salts such as nitrates, magnesium and potassium (accept 'nutrients'). Many students will say 'food' for question 3: challenge it, the plant makes its own food.

slides.title: Today
slides.notes: Read each goal aloud. Point to the key words box on the worksheet.

slides.title: Why does a plant eat flies?
slides.caption: A Venus flytrap. The trap shuts when a hair is touched twice.
slides.question: The Venus flytrap grows in bogs where the soil contains very few mineral salts. What does it get from a fly that it cannot get from the soil?
text: Talk to a partner. Then: suggest why a hair has to be touched more than once before the trap shuts.
slides.notes: The fly supplies mineral salts, especially nitrates (nitrogen for proteins) and potassium. The plant still makes its own glucose by photosynthesis; the fly is not its energy source. Touching twice stops the trap wasting energy shutting on raindrops or dust.

slides.title: What plants need from mineral salts

headers: What the plant uses it for
rows: making proteins, so cells can grow

text: Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen come from water and carbon dioxide.
Mineral salts dissolve in soil water and enter through the roots.
slides.key_idea: Mineral salts are not food: they are building materials. Nitrates build proteins; magnesium builds chlorophyll.
slides.notes: Students copy the table. Ask: what happens to photosynthesis in a plant short of magnesium? Less chlorophyll, so less energy captured, so less glucose and slower growth. This is Stretch 3 on the worksheet.

slides.title: Roots: collecting water and mineral salts
slides.caption: Root hairs on a seedling
text: Roots hold the plant in place and absorb water with dissolved mineral salts.
Roots are branched and spread out to reach water in a large volume of soil.
Root hair cells have a long extension: a large surface area to absorb water quickly.
Water passes to xylem vessels: long hollow tubes formed when chains of xylem cells die.
Xylem carries water and mineral salts up to the leaves.
slides.key_idea: Large surface area = faster absorption. Hollow dead cells = a pipe.
slides.notes: Hold a bunch of fine string next to a single thick rope: which has more surface? Root hairs work the same way. Xylem is made of dead cells: the end walls break down, leaving a continuous tube.

slides.title: The route of water through a plant
slides.text: Water is needed for photosynthesis, to keep leaves cool, and to fill cells so they stay firm.
slides.key_idea: Too little water: the cells sag, the leaves droop and the plant wilts. Water the plant and the cells fill again.
slides.notes: Trace the route aloud: soil water, root hair cell, xylem in the root, xylem in the stem, leaf cells, out through the stomata as water vapour (next lesson). Show a wilted and a watered pot plant if you have them.

slides.title: Inside a leaf
slides.text: Leaves are broad and thin. Which layer has the most chloroplasts, and why is it near the top?
slides.key_idea: Palisade cells sit near the upper surface, where there is most light, and are packed with chloroplasts.
slides.notes: Answer: the palisade layer, just under the clear upper epidermis, because light arrives from above. The spongy layer has air spaces for gases, the vein carries water in (xylem) and sugar out (phloem), and the stomata are mostly underneath. Next lesson looks at the stomata in detail.

slides.title: Leaves: catching light
slides.caption: Chloroplasts inside leaf cells (microscope)
text: Broad leaves have a large surface area to trap light.
Leaves are arranged so the upper ones do not shade the lower ones too much.
The epidermis makes a waxy cuticle that stops the leaf losing too much water.
Palisade cells contain many chloroplasts, where photosynthesis happens.
In dim light the chloroplasts move nearer the surface; in bright light they move away to avoid damage.
slides.key_idea: Shape fits function: broad and thin for light, a cuticle to keep water in, palisade cells full of chloroplasts.
slides.notes: Optional activity for the Do phase: trace a leaf on squared paper and count the squares to estimate its surface area. Compare a sun leaf and a shade leaf from the same tree: shade leaves are often larger and thinner.

slides.title: Quick check
slides.instruction: Mini whiteboards. One answer each, then we check.
questions: Which mineral salt supplies nitrogen for making proteins?
A plant has yellow leaves. Which element is it short of?
How are root hair cells adapted to absorb water quickly?
Which tissue carries water up the stem, xylem or phloem?
Which leaf cells contain the most chloroplasts?
slides.notes: Answers: nitrates; magnesium; a long extension gives a large surface area; xylem; palisade cells. Ask a student to say the difference between xylem (water up, dead cells) and phloem (sugar solution, living cells).

slides.title: Your turn
steps: Core: complete the table of what plants need, match the leaf parts, then fill the gaps on the route of water.
Stretch: explain the adaptations of xylem and root hair cells, wilting and recovery, and the yellow leaves.
Challenge: the Venus flytrap and how a leaf supplies its palisade cells.
Optional with your partner: trace a leaf on squared paper and estimate its surface area in cm².
slides.footer: Use the key words box. Every answer about an adaptation should say what the structure is like AND what that lets it do.
slides.notes: Model one adaptation answer on the board: 'Root hair cells have a long thin extension (what it is like), which gives a large surface area, so water is absorbed faster (what it does).' Insist on both halves.

slides.title: Wilt and recover
slides.prompt: A pot plant is left without water for a week and wilts. Two hours after watering it stands up straight again. Explain both changes.
slides.caption: A wilted plant
frames: Without water, the cells ___ so the leaves ___.
After watering, water travels from the ___ through the ___ to the leaves.
The cells fill up again and become ___.
slides.notes: Expected: without water the cells sag (lose their firmness) so the leaves droop; after watering, water is absorbed by root hair cells and carried up in the xylem; the cells fill with water, become firm, and hold the leaves up. Lesson 3 adds how water leaves through the stomata.

slides.title: Exit ticket
questions: Name the mineral salt a plant needs to make proteins.
How are root hair cells adapted to absorb water?
Why do palisade cells contain so many chloroplasts?
slides.notes: Answers: nitrates; a long extension gives a large surface area so water is absorbed quickly; they are near the top of the leaf where there is most light, and chloroplasts are where photosynthesis happens. Collect the strips.

slides.title: What we learned
slides.next: Gas exchange: how stomata let carbon dioxide in and oxygen and water vapour out.
points: Plants need nitrates (proteins), magnesium (chlorophyll) and potassium (absorbing water) from mineral salts in the soil.
Root hair cells have a large surface area; xylem vessels are hollow tubes of dead cells that carry water and mineral salts up.
Water is needed for photosynthesis, cooling and keeping cells firm; too little and the plant wilts.
Leaves are broad and thin, with a waxy cuticle and palisade cells packed with chloroplasts near the top.
slides.notes: Homework: Workbook page 17. Bring in a leaf next lesson if you want to look at its stomata under the microscope.

core.q: Complete the table to show how plants get what they need for growth. Use the word bank: air, soil water, respiration, photosynthesis, making proteins, making chlorophyll, absorbing water, keeping cells firm.
Match each part of a leaf to how it helps the plant. Draw a line.

right: carries water and mineral salts from the roots
stops the leaf losing too much water
allow gases to enter and leave the leaf
contain many chloroplasts, near the top where there is most light
carries dissolved sugars from the leaf to other parts of the plant

core.q: Complete the sentences about the route of water. Use the word bank.
gap_lines: Water enters the plant through ____________ cells, which have a large ____________ so they absorb water quickly.
The water travels up the root and stem in ____________ vessels, which are hollow tubes made from ____________ cells.
If a plant has too little water, its cells sag and the plant ____________.

stretch.q: Describe how each of these cells is adapted for its function. Say what the cell is like and what that lets it do.
A plant short of magnesium has yellow leaves and grows slowly. Explain why it grows slowly. Use the words chlorophyll, light and glucose.
Explain why water is important to a plant. Give three different reasons.

challenge.q: The Venus flytrap grows in bogs with very few mineral salts in the soil. It catches insects when the trigger hairs in its trap are touched more than once.

parts.text: Suggest why a trigger hair has to be touched more than once before the trap shuts.
State what the Venus flytrap gets from the insects, and explain why it might die without them even though it can photosynthesise.

challenge.q: Describe how a leaf is adapted to allow its palisade cells to get all the resources they need for photosynthesis: light, carbon dioxide and water.

worksheet.my_thinking: Some farmers grow lettuce in water with mineral salts dissolved in it, and no soil at all. Could this work? What would the plants still need, and where would it come from?
exit: Name the mineral salt a plant needs to make proteins.
How are root hair cells adapted to absorb water?
Why do palisade cells contain so many chloroplasts?

core: oxygen: air (and soil air for roots), respiration. carbon dioxide: air, photosynthesis. nitrate salts: soil water, making proteins. magnesium salts: soil water, making chlorophyll. potassium salts: soil water, absorbing water (roots). water: soil water, photosynthesis and keeping cells firm (also cooling).

palisade cells: contain many chloroplasts near the top; phloem: carries dissolved sugars from the leaf; xylem: carries water and mineral salts from the roots; stomata: allow gases to enter and leave; cuticle: stops the leaf losing too much water.
root hair; surface area; xylem; dead; wilts.
stretch: a) Xylem cells die and become hollow, and their end walls break down, so chains of them form long continuous tubes that carry water and mineral salts up the plant. b) Root hair cells have a long thin extension, which gives a large surface area, so they absorb water (with dissolved mineral salts) from the soil quickly.

Secure answer: magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll. With less chlorophyll (yellow leaves) the plant captures less energy from light, so photosynthesis is slower, less glucose is made, and there is less glucose for respiration and for building new cells, so growth is slow.

Any three: water is a reactant in photosynthesis; it keeps cells filled so leaves stay firm and the plant does not wilt; it keeps the leaves cool (evaporation); it carries dissolved mineral salts from the soil; it dissolves sugars so they can be moved in the phloem.
challenge: a) Shutting the trap uses energy; waiting for a second touch means it does not shut on raindrops or dust, only on an insect that is moving. b) The insects supply mineral salts, mainly nitrates for making proteins and potassium. The plant can make glucose by photosynthesis, but without nitrates it cannot make proteins (including enzymes) to grow and repair itself, and without potassium its roots cannot absorb water properly, so it could die.

Secure answer: light: the leaf is broad (large surface area) and thin, the upper epidermis is clear, and palisade cells are just under it where light is strongest. Carbon dioxide: stomata let it diffuse in, the spongy layer has air spaces so it reaches every cell, and the leaf is thin so the distance is short. Water: xylem in the veins brings water from the roots to the cells, and the waxy cuticle stops too much being lost.
exit: They have a long thin extension, which gives a large surface area, so water is absorbed quickly.
Photosynthesis happens in chloroplasts, and palisade cells are near the upper surface where there is most light.
answers.my_thinking: Yes (hydroponics). The plants still need water and dissolved mineral salts (from the solution), carbon dioxide and oxygen (from the air, and oxygen bubbled into the water for the roots) and light (sunlight or lamps). The soil only ever supplied water, mineral salts and support.
